A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MotionAgent and retain matching core methods, experiments and supplementary material. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout, supporting comparison despite substantial additions in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original MotionAgent benchmark results, a user study and component ablations, including the supplementary trajectory-plotting experiment.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds rethinking evaluations, adapter and model-component ablations, and complex/ambiguous-prompt experiments.

M1.justification: v2 introduces an optional rethinking feedback loop that inspects generated videos and corrects object trajectories and camera extrinsics before regeneration (Section 3.1.4). This substantively extends v1's generation procedure. Section 4.3.3 also describes an adaptation replacing Motion-I2V's Flow U-Net with MotionAgent-generated flow.

E1.justification: The VBench images and object/camera-motion tasks are retained. v2 adds evaluation scenarios using linguistically complex and ambiguous rewrites of the existing motion prompts (Section 9, Table 7). The newly stated 432 and 662 prompt counts do not establish expanded sampling relative to v1.

E2.justification: The published-method comparator sets in Tables 1–2 and the user study remain unchanged. Within the component comparisons, v2 adds an untuned-adapter control to Table 3 and alternative LLM/backbone variants in Table 4. The new prompt stress tests reuse existing CogVideoX and Pyramid Flow comparators.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce Qwen2, Llama3 and Motion-I2V configurations, an untuned-adapter control, and comparisons with rethinking enabled. Existing training hyperparameters, benchmark metrics and user-study design are retained. The added prompt counts and 1,500-rating total clarify existing experiments rather than establish changed sample sizes.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained localization, flow-composition and grid-selection ablations, v2 tests adapter fine-tuning, dependence on the LLM and video backbone, and rethinking effectiveness. Supplementary Sections 8–9 add feedback analysis and complex/ambiguous-prompt robustness tests; new cases examine motion correction, artifacts and dynamic degree.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The user study retains the same mean-ranking reporting. Clarifying its 1,500 ratings does not introduce a new statistical estimation or uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark rows, grid-selection scores and user-study rankings are retained, but substantial new results appear. Table 2 adds rethinking scores of 49.58/89.04/73.45 versus 45.69/77.76/65.10 without rethinking. Tables 3–4 and 7 add component and robustness findings. Table 6 reports rethinking camera accuracy of 87.02 versus 81.91, alongside dynamic degree of 15.38 versus 16.67.

T1.justification: v2 omits v1's explicit large-focal-length and zero-z-displacement assumptions and the depth-scaled xy-offset formula in Section 3.2.1. The remaining projection, flow and training-data equations are largely equivalent under renamed notation. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion now include feedback-based correction, and the introduction adds robustness/generalization claims. The three original contribution bullets and central claims about text-guided motion control and the motion benchmark remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 explains adapter tuning's importance and interprets rethinking as correcting motion and reducing artifacts, potentially sacrificing dynamism through shorter trajectories. It discusses degradation under ambiguous prompts. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation about LLM failures on particularly complex motion and its proposed fine-tuning remedy are removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-code link and substantial agent prompt templates covering trajectory plotting, camera generation and rethinking (Tables 8–10), including function parameters, coordinate conventions and output formats. It also documents benchmark prompt counts, the user-study rating total and per-frame Metric3D use during training-data preparation. These are disclosures, not evidence that existing experiments changed.

R1.justification: Related-work positioning expands substantially: v2 identifies Motionzero as the closest work and discusses additional joint-motion and 3D-aware approaches, including I2VControl, Motion Prompting and MotionCanvas. It acknowledges prior multi-motion control more explicitly and emphasizes its text-driven agent distinction. Generic LLM background and several associated references are removed.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain recognizable, with localized rewriting of related work and flow composition. Metric explanations move to supplementary Section 11, supplementary sections are reorganized, and front matter and acknowledgments change. Much of the original methodological and experimental prose is retained.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are revised to show feedback, qualitative comparisons are redistributed between the main text and supplement, and new motion-control and rethinking illustrations are added. Tables gain feedback and adapter-control entries, alongside new model, robustness and prompt-template tables. The user-study chart and grid-selection table are retained after relocation.

improvement.justification: The added adapter/backbone ablations and prompt-robustness tests strengthen empirical support, while the prompt templates improve reproducibility. Rethinking receives quantitative and visual validation, including its reduced-dynamism tradeoff. These benefits are tempered by removal of explicit geometric assumptions and the complex-motion limitation, yielding a limited net improvement.
